name: Beth Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will carry your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on an east side crew for Northgate Energy, the private company that runs the city's power. We meet at the yard at seven, load the truck, and spend the day in back lanes full of old trees and old poles, swapping transformers, fixing service drops to houses, sometimes down in the underground vaults. I'm a third-year apprentice, and I'm 58, so you can imagine the jokes. Before this I drove a school bus for 22 years. I came in through a Women into Trades programme when I was 55.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that it's real. A woman comes out in her dressing gown and says thank you because her fridge is humming again. What wears me out is the maths, honestly. Transformer calculations make my head spin, and I'm slower than the 20-year-olds. I've started asking one of those AI chat programmes to quiz me on the theory at night, and Joanne, the journeywoman I eat lunch with, checks my answers the next day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. I'm going to describe five pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a relief, and then I'd go back to my sandwich. I'd probably post something like, “Turns out the robots aren't coming for the back lanes.” My friends from the bus depot would laugh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I get my eight years. I came in late, so I'm planning to work to 66 to get anything decent from the pension. If nothing changes, I finish my apprenticeship, get my ticket and do the job till then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going. Pass my final exams next autumn, keep using the chat programme to drill the theory, and keep putting a bit away each month. Rosa and I would carry on as we are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like when the bus pulls in on time and nobody's thrown up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI a little already. In this picture, would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. It's handy for practice questions and for writing the odd email to the training office. It's like a patient tutor at midnight. But it's never once told me how to get a ladder past Mrs Kowalski's apple tree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about money at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd be fine. Rosa's at the central library, I'm on normal apprentice-to-qualified pay, and we've got about three months saved. Our big hope is to help our daughter Lucía with a deposit on a flat one day.

S0.say: She'd say it was a relief and go back to her lunch, maybe posting that the robots aren't coming for the back lanes. Her old friends from the bus depot would laugh along.
S0.think: Privately it means she gets the eight years she needs, working to 66 to build a decent pension after starting late. She'd finish her apprenticeship and stay in the job until then.
S0.do: Carries on: passes her final exams next autumn, keeps drilling the theory with an AI chat programme and saves a little each month. Keeps the household plans as they are.
S0.feel: Calm, like a school bus arriving on time without trouble.
S0.quote: It's like a patient tutor at midnight. But it's never once told me how to get a ladder past Mrs Kowalski's apple tree.
S0.fieldNote: Beth is already a light AI user, but only as a study aid for the maths she finds hard. Her pension plan depends on working to 66 after a late start, so stability is all she wants here. She is warm and funny and keeps comparing the work with her bus-driving years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company has to bring the workers along. At our union meeting I'd ask for a proper agreement: training on paid time, and no one pushed out because they're slower with the new stuff. I'd say it as the slow one, which helps, because nobody can say I'm just protecting myself from nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think our job changes but survives. Drones will check the lines, the computer will tell us which transformer is about to fail, and there'll be fewer emergency call-outs. I'm fine with that once I see it working. But I'm 58 and I'm the weakest on theory, so if they want fewer people, I'm on the list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for any course the company runs on the new systems, the minute the first crew shows it actually works. I'd ask Joanne to tell me honestly where I'm weakest. And I'd keep pushing the union to get it in writing, this coming year, before the changes start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, just watching the road more carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait till you see it work. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Marcus's crew on the north side uses a drone for three months and it finds real faults, I'm in. I did the same with the new bus routing system years back. I let the others find the bugs, then I learned it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter, not me. Lucía answers phones at an insurance call centre. That's the first job this kind of AI eats, isn't it? I'd tell her to start looking now, maybe even at an apprenticeship like her mum.

S1.say: She'd ask her union for an agreement covering paid training and protection for slower workers. She'd make the case openly as the slow learner on her crew.
S1.think: Privately she thinks the job changes but survives, with drones and smarter fault prediction. She's open to it once proven, but knows that at 58 and weakest on theory she'd be on any list for cuts.
S1.do: Signs up for company courses on new systems as soon as another crew proves they work, and asks a trusted journeywoman where she's weakest. Pushes the union to get an agreement in writing in the coming year.
S1.feel: Uneasy but steady, like watching the road more carefully.
S1.quote: I let the others find the bugs, then I learned it properly.
S1.fieldNote: Beth is a classic wait-until-proven adopter, and she has a concrete test in mind: another crew's three-month drone trial. Her union instincts and her honesty about being slow sit side by side. Her real worry jumps quickly to her daughter's call-centre job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need public ownership of the power grid and a share of the profits for the people who get replaced. I'd be at the protest outside the Northgate head office, with Rosa and her library friends. Online I'd share every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully? It's both of us at once. Rosa's library job and my line job, gone in the same two years, and Lucía's call centre before either. I switched careers at 55 because I thought this was safe. I'd be 60 with a half-built pension and three months in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, Rosa and I would sit at the kitchen table and go through every outgoing. We'd stop putting money aside for Lucía's deposit and put it into our own savings instead, aiming for six months by the end of the year. I'd join the union's campaign for a jobs guarantee and write to our city councillor, and I'd ask HR what the redundancy terms would be for someone with three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd be lying awake doing sums, like I did the year my first husband left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lucía about the deposit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the part that would hurt most. I'd say, sweetheart, we have to keep it for now, because if Mum and Rosa go under you'll be looking after us. She'd understand. She'd probably already be out of work herself by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short. Is there anything that time lets you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. It's long enough to panic and short enough that you can't retrain properly. If I started a new course tomorrow, the robots would finish it before me. So the time is for saving and for shouting, not for planning a new life.

S2.say: She'd call for public ownership of the grid and a share of profits for replaced workers, and join a protest outside her employer's head office. Online she'd share every petition.
S2.think: Privately she fears both household jobs and her daughter's would go within the same two years. She switched careers at 55 thinking line work was safe and would be 60 with a half-built pension and three months saved.
S2.do: Goes through every household bill with her partner in the first month and diverts the daughter's deposit fund into their own savings, aiming for six months by year end. Joins the union campaign for a jobs guarantee, writes to the city councillor and asks HR about redundancy terms.
S2.feel: Frightened and losing sleep over money.
S2.quote: It's long enough to panic and short enough that you can't retrain properly.
S2.fieldNote: What tips Beth into alarm is that both incomes in the house, plus her daughter's, would be hit at once. She sees two years as useless for retraining and good only for saving and protesting. Pulling back the deposit money for her daughter is the change that hurts her most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them. Train lineworkers to run and repair the robots, and keep a person in charge of every crew. I'd say it at the union, and I'd say it to anyone running for office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years puts me at 63 with my ticket and some pension. That's not great, but it's not a cliff. And I think there'll be a spell where somebody has to babysit the robots on the poles, and a careful old bus driver might be just the person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the apprenticeship first. Then, once there's a course on supervising the robot crews and somebody I trust says it's worth it, I'd take it, probably around year three. Rosa and I would save harder, maybe 200 more a month, and put Lucía's deposit on hold but not cancel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel I had my hands on the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take the course once someone you trust says it's worth it. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joanne. She's been on the tools fifteen years and she doesn't fall for anything. If she says the robot course is real, I'll do it. If she says it's a sales pitch, I won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the extra three years change for Rosa?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd have time to move from the library desk into something with people, maybe the council's adult learning service. She's been talking about it for years. Five years gives her a push without throwing her off the bus.

S3.say: She'd argue for using the five years to train lineworkers to run and repair the robots, with a person in charge of every crew. She'd say it to the union and to candidates for office.
S3.think: Privately she sees five years as a slope rather than a cliff: 63, qualified, with some pension. She suspects robots on poles will need careful human supervisors for a while, and thinks she could be one.
S3.do: Finishes the apprenticeship, then takes a course on supervising robot crews around year three once a trusted colleague vouches for it. Saves about 200 more a month and pauses, but doesn't cancel, her daughter's deposit fund.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with her hands on the wheel.
S3.quote: And I think there'll be a spell where somebody has to babysit the robots on the poles, and a careful old bus driver might be just the person.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Beth from defence to a cautious plan, with a clear trigger for retraining: a respected colleague's say-so. She sees value in her carefulness as a robot supervisor. She also imagines her partner using the time to change roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this decently, and the test is whether the people who lose their jobs share in what the machines earn. I'd vote on it and I'd say so at union meetings. I wouldn't be shouting, I'd be organising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me it's all right. I'd work to 66, retire in 2034 and miss the worst of it. Lucía is the one with a decade of working life in the way of it, and she's got time to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with the job and the pension plan. I'd pick up the new tools as the crews prove them, and help Lucía pay for an apprenticeship or a course in the next couple of years. And I'd go to the union's political meetings, the ones I usually skip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. It feels like a long trip with a map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a moment you picture in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My last day, in 2034, handing my belt to some young woman who came through the same programme. Maybe she'll be running a robot instead of climbing, but she'll still need someone to tell her which dogs on the east side bite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be calm, but you also want to organise. Which comes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They go together. I'm calm because there's time, and there's time because people like me use it. If nobody organises, ten years turns into two very quickly.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is enough to handle it decently, judged by whether displaced workers share what machines earn. She'd vote on it and organise rather than shout.
S4.think: Privately she expects to retire in 2034 at 66 and miss the worst. Her daughter has more at stake but also a decade to move.
S4.do: Keeps going with the job and pension plan and picks up new tools as crews prove them. Helps her daughter pay for an apprenticeship or course in the next couple of years and starts attending union political meetings.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, like a long trip with a map.
S4.quote: If nobody organises, ten years turns into two very quickly.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Beth is calm because her retirement lands before the change and her daughter has time. Her calm and her activism aren't in tension for her: organising is what keeps the time real. She pictures handing over to another woman from her training programme.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it hits Rosa, Lucía and me all at once and there's no time to turn. What would help is a jobs guarantee, or at least wages paid while people retrain, and the grid back in public hands so the savings come to all of us. And a pension rule that doesn't punish people who changed careers late.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask why a 55-year-old woman climbs poles. I did it because a bus seat was killing my back and I wanted something nobody could take off me. I'd hate to find out I was wrong about that.

headlineQuote: I did it because a bus seat was killing my back and I wanted something nobody could take off me.
portrait: Beth Alvarez is a 58-year-old third-year apprentice on an east side crew for Northgate Energy, a private city electricity company, after 22 years driving a school bus. She's progressive and union-minded, uses an AI chat programme now and then to drill the theory she finds hard, and adopts new tools once someone she trusts has proven them. AI Plateau and Steady Disruption leave her calm to uneasy. AGI in two years alarms her because her partner's library job, her daughter's call-centre job and her own would all be at risk at once. With five or ten years she settles into a careful plan of finishing her ticket, retraining to supervise robots if it's proven, and organising.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because it would hit her, her partner and her daughter all at once with no time to change course.
whatWouldHelp: A jobs guarantee or paid retraining, the grid back in public ownership so the savings are shared, and pension rules that don't punish late career changers.
